title: Recent Inflation Developments and Challenges for Research and Monetary Policymaking
summary: In this May 2016 speech at the Konstanz Seminar on Monetary Theory and Monetary Policy, former Cleveland Fed President Loretta Mester discussed recent inflation developments and the challenges they pose for researchers and policymakers. Mester noted that inflation had been running below the Fed's 2 percent target for some time, a phenomenon also observed in the UK and Euro area, and reviewed factors contributing to low inflation including weak global demand, declining energy and commodity prices, and US dollar appreciation.
key_points: The Fed established its explicit 2 percent inflation target in January 2012, measured by year-over-year PCE inflation, viewed symmetrically by the FOMC
By respective target measures, 2015 inflation was 0.20% in the UK (CPI), 0.25% in the Euro area (HICP), and 0.66% in the US (PCE)
Common factors contributing to low inflation globally included weak global demand post-financial crisis, declining energy/commodity prices, and US dollar appreciation

According to Fed Board staff SIGMA model simulations, a 10 percent rise in the real value of the dollar reduces core inflation by about 0.5 percent after one year, with partial reversal over the subsequent year
Dollar appreciation also reduces GDP with a lag, putting additional downward pressure on inflation
Mester emphasized that while inflation measurement, forecasting, and understanding transmission mechanisms remain challenging, these difficulties should not lead to policy nihilism
why_it_matters: This speech provides historical context on the low-inflation environment that characterized the post-Great Recession period through 2016. The SIGMA model estimates cited on dollar pass-through remain relevant for understanding inflation dynamics, though the specific inflation rates and economic conditions described are historical. The speech articulates the Fed's symmetric approach to its inflation target, which continues to inform current policy framework discussions.
macro_context: The speech contextualizes the low inflation environment of 2015-2016 as a global phenomenon affecting the US, UK, and Euro area. Key macro insight: dollar appreciation has significant and relatively quick effects on import prices and core inflation, with secondary effects through GDP growth. The speech was given prior to the Fed's December 2015 rate hike and discusses the environment that shaped early tightening deliberations.
important_numbers: 10 percent dollar appreciation leads to 0.5 percent core inflation decline after one year
January 2012: Fed established explicit inflation target
